This is a very small codebase — 5 files, ~130 lines total, zero third-party dependencies (only `node:http` and `node:crypto`). There's no `package.json`, no README, no tests, and it isn't under version control, so the source is the only documentation.

## The shape of it

A minimal JSON HTTP API arranged in four clean layers, each file depending only on the one below it:

```
server.js   HTTP listener + auth gate
   ↓
routes.js   method+path → handler table
   ↓
cache.js    LRU read-through (reads only)
   ↓
store.js    in-memory data with TTL
```

`auth.js` sits off to the side, used only by `server.js`.

## Request lifecycle

1. **`server.js:8`** — every request hits one handler. It calls `verifyToken` on the `Authorization` header first; no token, no entry (401). Nothing downstream ever re-checks auth, so this is the single gate.
2. **`routes.js:14`** — builds a key like `"GET /orders"` from the method and pathname, looks it up in `TABLE`. Miss → 404.
3. Handler runs, wrapped in `Promise.resolve(...)` so sync and async handlers are interchangeable. Resolve → 200 + JSON. Reject → 500 with the error message as the body.

Three endpoints exist: `GET /users`, `GET /orders`, `POST /orders`.

## The modules

**`auth.js`** — HMAC bearer tokens shaped `<userId>.<hexsig>`. `sign(userId)` is an HMAC-SHA256 of the user id under `AUTH_SECRET` (defaults to `'dev-secret'`). Verification recomputes the signature and compares with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. Note there's no expiry and no revocation — a token is valid forever as long as the secret holds. There's also no user lookup: the identity is whatever id is in the token.

**`routes.js`** — the table at line 7 is the whole routing story. Reads are wrapped in `cached(...)`; the write goes direct to the store. Handlers receive `(query, user)`, so `user.id` is how ownership is expressed — `GET /orders` and `POST /orders` are implicitly scoped to the caller.

**`cache.js`** — a 256-entry LRU using `Map` insertion order as the recency list: a hit deletes and re-inserts the key to bump it, and overflow evicts `lru.keys().next().value` (the oldest). Deliberately no TTL — the header comment says freshness is the store's job.

**`store.js`** — a `Map` of `{ value, expiresAt }` with a 15-minute TTL, lazily swept on read. Two key namespaces, `user:<id>` and `orders:<userId>`. Orders are stored as one array per user; `putOrder` reads the array, pushes, and writes back, which refreshes that user's TTL. Everything lives in process memory, so a restart is a full data wipe.

## Things worth knowing before you change anything

A few places where the code and its stated intent don't line up — I'd verify these against whatever your actual requirements are rather than assume they're deliberate:

- **The cache is never invalidated.** The comment at `routes.js:5` says writes "invalidate the affected keys," but `cache.js` exports only `cached` — there's no invalidate function and nothing calls one. So `POST /orders` updates the store while `GET /orders` keeps serving the stale pre-write array from the LRU, indefinitely (the cache has no TTL). This is the biggest gap I'd look at first.
- **There's no request body parsing.** `POST /orders` passes `q.body` (`routes.js:10`), but `parseQuery` only reads URL search params — it never touches the request stream. So a normal POST with a JSON body pushes `undefined` into the orders array. Writes only work at all via `?body=...` in the query string, as a string.
- **`GET /users` ignores the caller.** It looks up `q.id` from the query string, not `user.id`, so any authenticated user can fetch any user record. May be intended as an admin-ish endpoint, but it's unguarded.
- **A malformed token can crash the process.** `auth.js:16` compares `sig.length` in characters but `timingSafeEqual` compares bytes, so a signature with non-ASCII characters produces mismatched buffer lengths and throws. That throw is inside the raw `http` callback with no try/catch, which takes the server down.
- **Cache lifetime outlives store lifetime.** Store records expire at 15 minutes; cache entries don't expire at all. A cached read can outlive its backing record by a long way.

Want me to dig into any of these, or start fixing them?
